title: How Forests Clean the Air
summary: How trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen through photosynthesis, filter pollutants from the air, and why deforestation matters.
poll: Planting new trees can completely make up for the forests we lose to deforestation.

versions.title: Trees and Clean Air
versions.text:
Look up at a tall tree. It has green leaves. The leaves do a big job. They help clean the air we breathe.

Trees take in a gas from the air. We breathe out this same gas. Trees use the gas, plus water and sun, to grow. Then trees let out a new gas. We need this gas to live. We call it oxygen.

Sun gives each leaf power. The leaf uses the power and water to make food. This is how a tree grows and helps clean the air.

A forest is a big group of trees. A big forest can clean a lot of air. It can also trap dust from the air. The dust sticks to leaves and bark.

But many forests get cut down. When trees are gone, less air gets cleaned. The gas that trees would use stays in the air.

We can help forests. We can plant new trees. We can use less paper. We can speak up for trees near our homes.

Sunlight gives each leaf the power it needs. The leaf uses that power, plus water, to make food. This whole swap happens inside a tiny green leaf.

A forest is a big group of trees growing together. A large forest can clean a lot of air each day. Forests can also trap dust and smoke that float in the air. This dirt sticks to leaves, branches, and rough bark.

Sadly, people cut down many forests. When trees disappear, less air gets cleaned each day. The extra gas that trees would use just stays in the air.

Everyone can help forests in simple ways. We can plant new trees in our yards. We can use less paper at home and school. We can speak up for the trees near our own towns.

versions.title: Forests, Photosynthesis, and Clean Air
versions.text:
Consider a tall, leafy tree standing near your home, school, or a favorite park. Its green leaves perform an essential task every day. They help filter the very air that every person depends on.

Trees absorb a gas called carbon dioxide from the surrounding atmosphere, while people and animals exhale this same gas all day long. A tree uses this gas, together with water and sunlight, to grow strong, tall, and genuinely healthy. The tree then releases a different gas called oxygen back into the atmosphere, and every living thing within an ecosystem depends on oxygen in each breath it takes.

This remarkable exchange occurs inside a leaf, through a biological process that scientists call photosynthesis. Sunlight supplies each leaf with the energy needed for this process to occur, and the leaf then uses that captured energy, together with water drawn up through the roots, to transform carbon dioxide into food for the entire tree.

A forest is a vast collection of trees whose leafy canopy covers wide stretches of land. A large, thriving forest can filter a tremendous quantity of air each day, and forests can also trap tiny particles of dust, soot, and smoke, called pollutants, drifting through the surrounding air. This debris sticks firmly to leaves, branches, and bark.

Why does this matter so profoundly to scientists and environmental experts? When people clear away forests, an act called deforestation, considerably less of the harmful gas that factories and cars emit ever gets absorbed from the atmosphere. Trees can offset a portion of this steady emission, but only for as long as they remain standing. Once trees vanish, that offset disappears along with them, and the surplus gas remains trapped in the atmosphere instead.

Absolutely everyone, including every student, can help protect forests through simple actions. Plant new trees in your own yard. Use less paper at home and school. Speak up for the forests and their canopy that still grow near your own towns.

MID.prompt: Explain how cutting down forests, or deforestation, can lead to dirtier air. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I explained how each detail connects to dirtier air.
MID.modelAnswer: Cutting down forests can lead to dirtier air because it removes the very trees that would otherwise be absorbing harmful gas and trapping pollutants. One detail from the article is that trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during photosynthesis, so when a forest disappears through deforestation, that carbon dioxide simply stays in the air instead of being absorbed. A second detail is that forests trap tiny pollutants like dust, soot, and smoke on their leaves, branches, and bark, so without that forest, those same pollutants keep drifting freely through the air that people breathe. Because forests do both jobs at once, losing them makes the air noticeably dirtier.

HIGH.prompt: Some people argue that planting new trees can fully make up for the forests lost through deforestation. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that planting new trees can fully make up for forests lost through deforestation, because the article shows that a tree's ability to offset emissions depends on it actually standing and growing over time, not simply existing somewhere on a list. One piece of evidence is that trees absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis only while they are alive, so a newly planted sapling takes many years to absorb anywhere near as much as a mature tree that was part of an established canopy. A second piece of evidence is that forests also trap pollutants like dust and smoke across their bark and branches, a filtering ability tied to the size and density of the whole ecosystem, which a few scattered new trees cannot immediately replace. Because the benefits described in the article depend on time, scale, and a connected ecosystem, newly planted trees can help but cannot instantly offset what a mature forest provided.
